'''James Andrew Clarkson''' (7 February 1906 – 6 June 1970) was an American mathematician and professor of mathematics who specialized in [[number theory]]. He is known for proving inequalities in [[Hölder condition#Hölder spaces|Hölder spaces]], and derived from them, the [[uniform convexity]] of {{math|[[Lp spaces|<var>''L''<sup>p</sup></var> spaces]]}}. His proofs are known in mathematics as [[Clarkson's inequalities]]. He was an operations' analyst during World War II, and was awarded the Medal of Freedom for his achievements. He wrote ''First reader on game theory'', and many of his academic papers have been published in several scientific journals.  He was an invited speaker at the 1932 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] (ICM) in Zürich.

==Life==
Originally from [[Massachusetts]], in 1934 he received the Ph.D. in mathematics from [[Brown University]], with the dissertation entitled ''On Definitions of Bounded Variation for Functions of Two Variables, On Double Riemann–Stieltjes Integrals'' under the supervision of advisor [[Clarence Raymond Adams]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=4290}}</ref>

In 1943, he was assigned as a bombing analyst at the Bombing Accuracy Subsection of the Operational Research Section (ORS) at the Headquarters Eighth Air Force division of the United States Air Force, alongside other mathematicians like Frank M. Stewart, J. W. T. Youngs, Ray E. Gilman, and W. J. Youden. He later received the Medal of Freedom.<ref name="century">{{cite book|author-link1=Richard Askey|author1=Richard A. Askey|author2=Uta C. Merzbach|author2-link= Uta Merzbach |title=A century of mathematics in America. 1(1988)|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8KnZjdBlw14C|access-date=8 January 2013|year=1989|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-0124-6|lccn=88022155|page=380|chapter=The Mathematical Scene, 1940–1965}}</ref><ref name=analysis>{{cite book |last= McArthur|first= C. W.|title= Operations Analysis in the U.S. Army: Eighth Air Force in World War II.|year= 1990|publisher= American Mathematical Society |isbn= 9780821801581|lccn= 90000829}}</ref>

From 1940 to 1948 he held a [[Tenure (academic)|tenured]] appointment in the Department of Mathematics in the [[University of Pennsylvania]]<ref name="UpennTenured">{{cite web|url=http://www.math.upenn.edu/History/tenured_faculty_1899-.html|title=Tenured Faculty 1899 –|publisher=University of Pennsylvania|access-date=8 January 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130106234657/http://www.math.upenn.edu/History/tenured_faculty_1899-.html|archive-date=6 January 2013}}</ref> and then from 1949 to 1970 he held a professorship at [[Tufts University]].<ref>{{cite web |url        =http://provost.tufts.edu/institutionalresearch/files/2011-2012-Fact-Book-for-Web.pdf |title      =Tufts University Fact Book 2011–2012 |publisher  =Tufts University |access-date =7 January 2013}}</ref>

Most of his academic papers and contributions have been published by the [[American Mathematical Society]], and ''[[Duke Mathematical Journal]]''.
